clue.text: Bananas British Airways put at the front of gate in stylish container

parts.note: a bunch of bananas growing together is called a hand
the airline's standard abbreviation

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of gate

explanation.surface: An odd scene of bananas and an airline at a departure gate, inside some fashionable luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like an anagram signal meaning crazy, but it is a noun: bananas grow in clusters called hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A handbag is a fashion accessory, a smart little bag for carrying belongings.

clue.text: Beginning to fall, the young boxer loses head, becoming angry

indicators.note: losing the head means the first letter of the word is removed
in a down entry the first letter drops to the bottom, so the word's start moves to its end

parts.note: THE with its first letter moved to the end
a young boxer dog is a PUP; without its first letter

explanation.surface: A young boxer takes a fall, gets knocked on the head and loses his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: The boxer is a breed of dog, so a young one is a pup.
explanation.definitionFit: Being het up is an informal idiom for being agitated or worked up, close to anger.

clue.text: Some lingo freshly coined

indicators.note: doing something freshly means making it anew, so the letters are made over in a new arrangement

parts.note: the nine letters taken as fodder

explanation.surface: A remark on new slang just entering the language.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: a newly coined bit of language.
explanation.definitionFit: A neologism is a newly invented word or expression, exactly some fresh-minted language.

clue.text: Dance by topless simpleton that takes one's breath away

indicators.note: with no top, a down word loses its first letter

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance
LOON, a fool, with its first letter removed

explanation.surface: A dance partnered by a scantily clad fool proves breathtaking.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is literal: you blow your breath into a balloon to inflate it.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflating a balloon uses up the air in your lungs, so it literally takes one's breath.

clue.text: Bubbly and happy crowds around Great Britain?

indicators.note: to crowd around something is to surround it on all sides

parts.note: gay in its older sense of cheerful
the SS Great Britain is Brunel's famous steamship, preserved in Bristol

explanation.surface: A cheerful, effervescent crowd gathers around the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: Great Britain is not GB here: the question mark points to the ship, whose name carries the prefix SS (steamship).
explanation.definitionFit: Something gassy is full of gas bubbles, so fizzy or bubbly.

clue.text: Hot guy you once dated said something unoriginal

parts.note: a former partner is an ex

indicators.note: something said is spoken, so a word that only sounds right is wanted

parts.note: something cited is quoted from another source, hence unoriginal

explanation.surface: A tale of an attractive former boyfriend whose chat-up lines were second-hand.
explanation.walkthrough: CITED and SIGHTED are pronounced alike; the cited word is the one that fits 'unoriginal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot can mean aroused or worked up, a sense shared with excited.

clue.text: Harry — 'I'm red and pale of skin'

indicators.note: to harry is to harass and disturb, so these letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Harry reports that his complexion is blotchy, both flushed and pallid.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry looks like a name introducing a quote, but it is the verb meaning harass.
explanation.definitionFit: The epidermis is the outer layer of the skin, so epidermal means relating to the skin.

clue.text: Politician enthralled by firm bottom's breadth

indicators.note: someone enthralled is held captive, so this word sits held inside the next

parts.note: CO is short for company
Member of Parliament
American slang for the backside

explanation.surface: A politician admires the width of a toned backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Compass can mean range or scope, the full extent of something, which is its breadth.

clue.text: This endless, empty road leads to a pass, just

indicators.note: having no end means the final letter is cut off

parts.note: THIS without its last letter

indicators.note: emptied of its middle, only the outside letters of the word remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of road

explanation.surface: Directions along a deserted road that barely gets you to a mountain pass.
explanation.walkthrough: A pass here is an exam result, not a mountain gap: a third is the lowest class of British honours degree.
explanation.definitionFit: A third-class degree in the UK is the lowest honours award, a bare pass.

clue.text: That worn by one who's been called?

definitions.text: That worn by one who's been called?

parts.words: That worn by one who's been called?
parts.note: surface reading: something worn by a pet that has been given a name or summoned
setter's reading: a priest who has received a calling to the ministry

explanation.walkthrough: Called suggests an animal summoned by name, but it means having a vocation; clergy wear the white collar of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: The stiff white band worn by clergy is nicknamed after the collar a pet wears.

clue.text: What's charged upon a bridge crossing river?

definitions.text: What's charged upon a bridge crossing river?

indicators.note: something crossing a river spans it, so here one word stretches across the other

parts.note: a toll is a fee for using a bridge
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A question about fees for using a bridge over a river.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole, the clue recalls the troll in Three Billy Goats Gruff, who demands payment from anyone crossing his bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: In folk tales a troll lurks under a bridge and exacts a price from travellers who cross it.

clue.text: Carol's hugging some bloke and Solomon's dancing

indicators.note: a word hugging others wraps its arms around them, so they go inside it

parts.note: to carol is to sing
a man referred to as him
Solomon is the setter, so his is my

explanation.surface: Carol embraces a man while the setter takes to the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Carol looks like a woman's name but is the verb; setters refer to themselves by their pseudonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To shimmy is to dance shaking the shoulders and hips, so shimmying is a form of dancing.

clue.text: Model for books about nature

parts.note: pro means in favour of

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: the Old Testament books
nature in the sense of kind or sort

explanation.surface: A sample design for a series of nature books.
explanation.definitionFit: A prototype is the first version from which others are developed, a working model.

clue.text: Sound emerging from car when disc's put on

indicators.note: one thing put on another is attached after it, so the pieces are joined end to end

parts.note: a German car make
a disc is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: Music plays from the car stereo once a CD is inserted.
explanation.definitionFit: Audio is the general term for recorded or transmitted sound.

clue.text: Character with money, but not love, is smoking pot

indicators.note: love is zero in tennis, and 'not' it means that round letter is taken out

parts.note: a letter of the Greek alphabet
MONEY with its O removed

explanation.surface: A wealthy but loveless person turns to cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: Pot suggests cannabis; here it is the pot of a smoking chimney stack. Love is O, as in tennis scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimney stack topped with a pot carries smoke out of a building, so it is a smoking pot.

clue.text: Charlie, Oscar, Henry, Abi and Edward lived together

parts.note: NATO alphabet code word for C
NATO alphabet code word for O
henry is the unit of inductance, symbol H
taken as written
Ted is a familiar form of Edward

explanation.surface: A list of five housemates who shared a home.
explanation.definitionFit: To cohabit is to live together as partners without being married.

clue.text: Place either end of yak before another beast of burden

parts.note: read literally: the end letters of yak are Y or K
a Shire is a heavy draught horse; 'another' because a yak is one too

explanation.surface: Describing a yak followed by some other pack animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Either end' reads as a selection instruction, but taken word for word it spells Y, OR, K.
explanation.definitionFit: Yorkshire is a large county in northern England, a geographical place.

clue.text: Masculine American I see alongside Jolson in The Jazz Singer?

parts.note: grammatical abbreviation
abbreviation for the United States
taken as written
the letter C sounds like see
Al Jolson, star of the 1927 film

explanation.surface: A manly American observing Al Jolson on screen in the famous film.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows the definition is by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jazz Singer, the first feature-length talkie, is a film full of songs, an example of a musical.

clue.text: Record from jazzman? A piece worked on by the Carpenters, reportedly

parts.note: cat is old jazz slang for a musician
taken as written

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.words: piece worked on by the Carpenters
parts.note: carpenters work with pieces of timber

explanation.surface: A jazz musician's album, with a track recorded by the pop duo the Carpenters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Carpenters suggest Karen and Richard's band; here they are woodworkers. Said aloud the pieces run together as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A catalogue is a systematic list or register, a record of items.

clue.text: The rams disperse — one's put in a cage

indicators.note: things that disperse scatter in all directions, so the letters scatter into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A flock of rams scatters and one of them gets penned in.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamster is a small rodent pet usually kept in a cage.

clue.text: A volatile artist may lose this article … paint?

parts.words: A volatile artist may lose this
parts.note: a hot-headed artist may lose his temper
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A temperamental painter might lose control over a pot of paint.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempera is a paint made by binding pigment with egg yolk, used by Renaissance painters.

clue.text: Let fly at half-cut gangster that won't easily crack

indicators.note: cut in half means the front half of the word is chopped away, leaving the back

parts.note: to lob is to throw high
the second half of gangster

explanation.surface: Someone lashes out at a drunken mobster who will not break under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for drunk, but here it means cut in half. 'Won't easily crack' sounds like a tough criminal, but it is the hard shell.
explanation.definitionFit: A lobster's thick armoured shell is notoriously hard to break open.

clue.text: Crazy people making love

definitions.meaning: second meaning: those who bonk, British slang for having sex

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is a jokey literal reading: bonk is British slang for having sex, so bonkers are people doing it.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective is slang for mad, while the whimsical noun names people having sex.

clue.text: Feel dozy? Turn off the lights

definitions.note: read as the phrase BE DIM
definitions.meaning: first meaning, split as two words

explanation.surface: Feeling sleepy, someone switches off the lamps.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half needs the answer split into two words; dozy in British English can mean stupid as well as sleepy.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedim is a literary verb meaning to make dark or obscure, as switching off lamps does.

clue.text: Put oil on to remove poster from the top of building

indicators.note: removing one word from another takes those letters out of it

parts.note: a building is identified by its address
an advertisement, as on a poster

explanation.surface: Instructions to lubricate something in order to peel a poster off a building.
explanation.walkthrough: The poster's letters come off the start of the longer word.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress a salad is to add oil and vinegar to it.

clue.text: Bed-wetter laundering the ends of pink polyester eiderdown with Persil

indicators.note: laundering churns things about in a wash, so the letters are tumbled into a new order
the end of each word is its final letter, so only those are kept

parts.note: last letter
last letter
last letter
a British washing powder brand, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who wets the bed washes the pink duvet with detergent.
explanation.walkthrough: Bed-wetter sounds like a child with an accident; the bed is a flower bed. Persil is a well-known British washing powder.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden sprinkler sprays water over flower beds, so it wets beds.

clue.text: What Scotsman drinks in the Betty Ford Center?

definitions.note: the clinic, standing for the treatment given there

indicators.note: someone who drinks takes something inside himself

parts.note: Rab is a Scottish short form of Robert
eh is a request to repeat, like what?

explanation.walkthrough: The Betty Ford Center is a well-known American clinic for treating alcohol and drug dependency.
explanation.definitionFit: Rehab is short for rehabilitation, the addiction treatment that the Betty Ford Center provides.

clue.text: Reinterpret Chaplin's boxing gag

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.walkthrough: Gag suggests a Chaplin joke, but it is the verb meaning heave.

clue.text: I threw the wobbly for that reason

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.definitionFit: Therewith is a formal word meaning with that or as a result of that, so for that reason.

clue.text: One fat lady lifting both ends of barbells?

clue.text: Princess's contentment to clap?

clue.text: Petition the leaders of Shugborough Estate to cut tree

parts.note: first letters of the two words
